label: The 27 Lines on a Cubic Surface
notes: Open the chapter. We reach one of the jewels of classical geometry. The deck follows printed pages 109 through 120 and shows that every smooth cubic surface in projective three-space contains exactly twenty-seven straight lines, develops the blow-up model that explains them, and surveys the rich symmetry hidden in their configuration.

label: Cubic Surfaces
notes: Introduce the smooth cubic surface as the zero set of a homogeneous cubic in projective three-space. It is a two-dimensional variety, far richer than a curve, and the natural place where lines on a surface become an interesting question. Counting and locating these lines is the central problem the chapter solves completely.

label: The Count of Twenty-Seven
notes: State the theorem of Cayley and Salmon: a smooth cubic surface contains exactly twenty-seven lines, no more and no fewer. The number is the same for every smooth cubic, an instance of how algebraic geometry produces sharp universal counts. Establishing both existence and exactness requires genuine argument, not mere parameter counting.

label: The Blow-up Model
notes: Explain why the lines exist. A smooth cubic surface is the blow-up of the projective plane at six points in general position. The twenty-seven lines arise as the six exceptional curves, the fifteen lines joining pairs of the points, and the six conics through five of them, accounting for the count exactly through this elegant model.

label: Symmetry of the Configuration
notes: Reveal the hidden structure. The twenty-seven lines meet in a highly symmetric pattern whose symmetry group is the Weyl group of the exceptional root system E6, of order fifty-one thousand eight hundred forty. Special configurations like double-sixes organize the lines and link this geometry to deep parts of group theory and representation theory.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter and the course. Every smooth cubic surface carries exactly twenty-seven lines, explained by realizing the surface as the plane blown up at six general points, and their configuration encodes the symmetry of the E6 root system. This classical gem shows the explicit power of the machinery built across the whole book.
